refsect1.title: DESCRIPTION
refsect1.para: Each unit runs in its own control group (a lightweight container), see cgroups 7 for more information.

Running units may or may not have a restart or a reload capability. restart the unit to define its restart command. reload requires the unit to define its reload command. Only units that are already started can be restarted or reloaded. What a restart or a reload does depends on the unit; generally a restart involves a brief interruption in functionality, but a reload typically maintains functionality while the unit updates itself.
These commands wait until the unit starts, stops, restarts, or reloads. An optional --nowait results in the command completing immediately, without waiting for the operation to finish.

Units are either masked, disabled, or enabled. These commands change the units' state. A masked unit never gets started manually or automatically, and starting it fails. Both disabled and enabled units are startable. The only difference between a disabled or an enabled unit is that an enabled unit gets automatically started as a result of some other unit starting, typically when the system starts, see
vera.runlevels 8
. Disabled units do not, but they are startable directly by themselves, on demand.
Newly installed units are disabled by default.

note.para: Not all units define which runlevel they're enabled for. If not, enabling or disabling the unit produces no functional difference.
Enabling or disabling a unit may not be related to runlevels, see for more information.

The enable, disable and mask commands work differently with units that get created by the inittab command (see ) for /etc/rc.d scripts. The sysvinit package checks the scripts' permissions and only runs executable scripts.
inittab creates a system/rc.M/name unit for these. The mask command is disabled for these units. The enable and disable commands modify the corresponding script's executable permissions.

These units are not directly enabled in any particular runlevel. The /etc/rc.d/rc.M script checks each script's permissions and (the on-the-fly modified script) starts the corresponding unit if it's executable, and the different behavior of enable and disable ends up having the same result as with regular units.

refsect1.para: The freeze command pauses all processes in the unit. The processes are not killed or removed, they just stop running. The thaw command resumes normal operation of the named unit.

refsect2.title: ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES
refsect2.para: Commands executed by vera (namely the starting and stopping commands) inherit the following environment variables, in addition to the ones that are set by the setenv command (and recorded in @ENVIRONCONFIG@).

listitem.para: The default path is /usr/local/sbin:/usr/sbin:/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin. Any non-default vera installation directory gets prepended to this default path.
The path to the system console device in /dev.
vera's version, for compatibility with init.
The current and possibly the previous runlevel (the one-character init alias), for compatibility with init.

refsect2.para: The setenv and unsetenv commands update additional environment variables for all commands started by vera. These commands update the @ENVIRONCONFIG@ file that sets the environment variables for all commands started by vera.

refsect2.title: The status command
refsect2.para: This command shows a list of all units (or just the units given as optional parameters), their current state, and their processes. status omits stopped units by default and units that are started but no longer have any processes (targets). The --all option includes started units without any processes. --stopped also includes stopped units (so --all is not truly all of them, as stopped processes are not included). The --stopped option is implied if any units are given as parameters.

--dependencies lists all units' dependencies (which all other units it requires, its required by, and which ones must be started or stopped first, as calculated from the unit's specification, see below). The --terse produces a compact status, one container per line, in a parsable format.

--resources also shows the unit's set resources, see
vera.extras 8
for more information.
status reads unit specifications from their directories (see ), the output may be incomplete if the running userid does not have permissions to access them.

row.entry: This unit is stopped and is not running
This unit has not started yet and is waiting for other units to start first; it starts after those units are fully started
This unit is starting, but has not finished starting
This unit is waiting to be restarted after it failed to start too many times
This unit is started and is running
This unit is waiting for other units to stop; it stops after those units finish stopping
This unit is in the process of stopping

refsect2.para: A manual annotation indicates that this unit is being started manually, by a vlad start command; otherwise it's started in order to start another unit.
The terse option shows a subset of the above information and formats the units in a compact list, one unit per line. Each line contains a list of field=value tuples, with colons as separators:

listitem.para: Whether the unit is marked as enabled.
How long the unit's starting or stopping script is running, in seconds. This is shown only if a starting or a stopping script is currently running.
How long the unit is running, in seconds. This is shown if the unit is in a started state.
A quoted list of space-delimited process ids in the unit's container, if there are any.

refsect2.para: This format is amenable to shell scripts:

informalexample.programlisting: # eval `vlad status --terse system/inittab/c1 | tr ':' '\012'` # echo $name system/inittab/c1 # echo $state started # echo $pids 1202 1223 1237 1220

note.para: There's no output from vlad status if the given container does not exist or if it's suppressed by the absence of --all and --stopped. Therefore any existing values of these shell variables remain unchanged.
This is also true for variables corresponding to names of values that are not always included in the output (which also includes pids!). Caveat emptor.
